claim: EED inactivation in the postnatal heart (EedCKO) caused lethal dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: EED (embryonic ectoderm development) inactivation in the postnatal heart (EedCKO) caused lethal dilated cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing heart dysfunction, survival curves, and histopathological examination in EedCKO mice.

claim: Gene upregulation in EedCKO was not coupled with loss of H3K27me3.
source: Surprisingly, gene upregulation in EedCKO was not coupled with loss of H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing H3K27me3 levels at upregulated genes and ChIP-qPCR validation.

claim: The activating histone mark H3K27ac increased in EedCKO.
source: Rather, the activating histone mark H3K27ac increased.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and ChIP-seq data showing increased H3K27ac levels in EedCKO.

claim: EED interacted with histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: EED interacted with histone deacetylases (HDACs) and enhanced their catalytic activity.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing EED-HDAC interaction.

claim: EED enhanced HDAC catalytic activity.
source: EED interacted with histone deacetylases (HDACs) and enhanced their catalytic activity.
evidence: Supported by in vitro deacetylase activity assays showing EED augmented HDAC2 activity.

claim: HDAC overexpression normalized EedCKO heart function.
source: HDAC overexpression normalized EedCKO heart function and expression of derepressed genes.
evidence: Supported by AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments showing restored heart function and gene expression.

claim: HDAC overexpression normalized expression of derepressed genes in EedCKO.
source: HDAC overexpression normalized EedCKO heart function and expression of derepressed genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data showing normalized gene expression after HDAC1/2 overexpression.

claim: EED has a non-canonical, H3K27me3-independent repressive mechanism essential for normal heart function.
source: Our results uncovered a non-canonical, H3K27me3-independent EED repressive mechanism that is essential for normal heart function.
evidence: Supported by data showing gene derepression without H3K27me3 loss and rescue without H3K27me3 restoration.

claim: Organ dysfunction due to epigenetic dysregulation can be corrected by epigenetic rewiring.
source: Our results further illustrate that organ dysfunction due to epigenetic dysregulation can be corrected by epigenetic rewiring.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing functional correction without restoring the original epigenetic landscape.

claim: EedCKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency.
source: EedCKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency, suggesting a lack of embryonic lethality, but most died over the first 3 months of life (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival data showing normal birth rates but postnatal lethality.

claim: Most EedCKO mice died over the first 3 months of life.
source: EedCKO mice were born at the expected Mendelian frequency, suggesting a lack of embryonic lethality, but most died over the first 3 months of life (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve data.

claim: EedCKO mice had left ventricular dilatation by echocardiography.
source: By echocardiography, EedCKO mice had left ventricular dilatation and progressive systolic dysfunction (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements.

claim: EedCKO mice had progressive systolic dysfunction by echocardiography.
source: By echocardiography, EedCKO mice had left ventricular dilatation and progressive systolic dysfunction (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements showing reduced fractional shortening.

claim: Histopathological examination confirmed massive cardiomegaly in EedCKO mice.
source: Histopathological examination confirmed massive cardiomegaly (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by heart to body weight ratio and histological analysis.

claim: The heart failure marker Nppa was strongly upregulated in EedCKO mice.
source: The expression level of the heart failure marker Nppa, encoding atrial natriuretic factor, was strongly upregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR measurements of Nppa expression.

claim: EedCKO mice that survived to 2 months of age had substantial CM hypertrophy.
source: EedCKO mice that survived to 2 months of age had substantial CM hypertrophy and cardiac fibrosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and cell size quantification.

claim: EedCKO mice that survived to 2 months of age had cardiac fibrosis.
source: EedCKO mice that survived to 2 months of age had substantial CM hypertrophy and cardiac fibrosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by Mason Trichrome staining showing fibrotic tissue.

claim: Eed is essential for neonatal heart maturation.
source: These results show that Eed is essential for neonatal heart maturation and that its inactivation in CMs causes lethal dilated cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypic consequences of Eed inactivation in postnatal cardiomyocytes.

claim: Eed inactivation in CMs causes lethal dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: These results show that Eed is essential for neonatal heart maturation and that its inactivation in CMs causes lethal dilated cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Supported by survival, echocardiography, and histopathological data.

claim: Cardiac Eed inactivation globally decreased H3K27me3 level in CMs.
source: As expected, cardiac Eed inactivation globally decreased H3K27me3 level in CMs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Eed inactivation reduced the number of regions enriched for H3K27me3 across the genome from 49991 to 7095.
source: Accordingly, Eed inactivation reduced the number of regions enriched for H3K27me3 across the genome from 49991 to 7095 (Figure 1I and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by H3K27me3 ChIP-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: 863 genes were upregulated in EedCKO cardiomyocytes.
source: We identified 863 upregulated and 392 downregulated genes in EedCKO (fold change >1.5 or <0.67 and adjusted p-value<0.05; Figure 1J and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: 392 genes were downregulated in EedCKO cardiomyocytes.
source: We identified 863 upregulated and 392 downregulated genes in EedCKO (fold change >1.5 or <0.67 and adjusted p-value<0.05; Figure 1J and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Slow-twitch myofiber genes were significantly upregulated in EedCKO heart.
source: Remarkably, we found that slow-twitch myofiber genes, such as Tnnt1, Tnni1, Myh7, Mybpc1, Myl9, Myl7, Myl4, Mybpc2, and Acta1, were significantly upregulated in EedCKO heart (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing increased expression of these genes.

claim: The upregulated genes in EedCKO were significantly enriched for gene ontology terms related to skeletal muscle genes.
source: Indeed, the upregulated genes were significantly enriched for gene ontology terms related to skeletal muscle genes (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Normal cardiac function requires proper expression of cardiac sarcomere genes and repression of skeletal muscle and slow-twitch myofiber genes.
source: Normal cardiac function requires proper expression of cardiac sarcomere genes and repression of skeletal muscle and slow-twitch myofiber genes (Frey et al., 2000; Montgomery et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2015), suggesting that abnormal expression of these genes contributes to weak cardiac contraction in EedCKO mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Abnormal expression of skeletal muscle and slow-twitch myofiber genes contributes to weak cardiac contraction in EedCKO mice.
source: Normal cardiac function requires proper expression of cardiac sarcomere genes and repression of skeletal muscle and slow-twitch myofiber genes (Frey et al., 2000; Montgomery et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2015), suggesting that abnormal expression of these genes contributes to weak cardiac contraction in EedCKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of upregulated skeletal muscle genes and cardiac dysfunction in EedCKO.

claim: About half of the upregulated genes (49.71%) were occupied by EED at their TSSs in WT.
source: About half of the upregulated genes (49.71%), including 7 of 14 upregulated skeletal muscle genes, were occupied by EED at their TSSs in WT.
evidence: Supported by EED ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: 7 of 14 upregulated skeletal muscle genes were occupied by EED at their TSSs in WT.
source: About half of the upregulated genes (49.71%), including 7 of 14 upregulated skeletal muscle genes, were occupied by EED at their TSSs in WT.
evidence: Supported by EED ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Only 8.42% of downregulated genes were bound by EED and H3K27me3.
source: Unlike upregulated genes, only 8.42% of downregulated genes were bound by EED and H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Gene upregulation (derepression) rather than downregulation is the predominant, direct effect of EED deficiency.
source: These findings suggest that gene upregulation (derepression) rather than downregulation is the predominant, direct effect of EED deficiency, and that repression of skeletal muscle genes is a key direct role of EED in adult heart.
evidence: Inferred from the higher proportion of upregulated genes bound by EED compared to downregulated genes.

claim: Repression of skeletal muscle genes is a key direct role of EED in adult heart.
source: These findings suggest that gene upregulation (derepression) rather than downregulation is the predominant, direct effect of EED deficiency, and that repression of skeletal muscle genes is a key direct role of EED in adult heart.
evidence: Inferred from EED occupancy at skeletal muscle genes and their upregulation in EedCKO.

claim: EED inactivation reduced the median H3K27me3 signal only of the quartile of genes with highest H3K27me3 occupancy in wild type.
source: This analysis showed that EED inactivation reduced the median H3K27me3 signal only of the quartile of genes with highest H3K27me3 occupancy in wild type.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of H3K27me3 ChIP-seq signal stratified by baseline occupancy.

claim: The median H3K27me3 signal in the remaining three quartiles of upregulated genes was not significantly altered by EED inactivation.
source: Surprisingly, the median H3K27me3 signal in the remaining three quartiles of upregulated genes was not significantly altered by EED inactivation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of H3K27me3 ChIP-seq signal.

claim: The aggregate H3K27me3 signal at the promoters of the 863 upregulated genes was not reduced in EedCKO.
source: Consistent with this analysis, the aggregate H3K27me3 signal at the promoters of the 863 upregulated genes was not reduced in EedCKO, while it was lower in EedCKO at the unchanged and downregulated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2N).
evidence: Supported by aggregate plot analysis of H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data.

claim: Cluster C1 contained only 252 of 863 upregulated genes (29%) in EedCKO.
source: Cluster C1, which matches the canonical view in which gene derepressed is association with loss of H3K27me3 (Margueron et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2008; Boyer et al., 2006), contained only 252 of 863 upregulated genes (29%) in EedCKO.
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of upregulated genes based on H3K27me3 changes.

claim: 4731 of 10,024 expressed genes (47%) had reduced promoter H3K27me3.
source: In comparison, 4731 of 10,024 expressed genes (47%) had reduced promoter H3K27me3, indicating lack of enrichment of H3K27me3 loss among upregulated genes.
evidence: Supported by genome-wide analysis of H3K27me3 changes.

claim: The majority of gene upregulation that occurs with Eed inactivation occurs without loss of H3K27me3.
source: Togerther, these analyses indicate that the majority of gene upregulation that occurs with Eed inactivation occurs without loss of H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by multiple analyses of H3K27me3 ChIP-seq data and ChIP-qPCR validation.

claim: Upregulation of most genes in EedCKO, including the derepressed skeletal muscle genes, was not accompanied by loss of H3K27me3.
source: Overall, these results indicate that upregulation of most genes in EedCKO, including the derepressed skeletal muscle genes, was not accompanied by loss of H3K27me3, as expected by the canonical model of EED repression via 'writing' of repressive H3K27me3 marks (Margueron et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by comprehensive ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR analysis.

claim: Eed inactivation markedly increased total histone H4 acetylation in purified EedCKO CMs.
source: Immunoblotting of purified EedCKO CMs showed that Eed inactivation markedly increased total histone H4 acetylation and acetylation of histone H3 at K9 and K27 (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Eed inactivation markedly increased acetylation of histone H3 at K9 in purified EedCKO CMs.
source: Immunoblotting of purified EedCKO CMs showed that Eed inactivation markedly increased total histone H4 acetylation and acetylation of histone H3 at K9 and K27 (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Eed inactivation markedly increased acetylation of histone H3 at K27 in purified EedCKO CMs.
source: Immunoblotting of purified EedCKO CMs showed that Eed inactivation markedly increased total histone H4 acetylation and acetylation of histone H3 at K9 and K27 (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Acute siRNA-mediated Eed knockdown in the HL-1 CM-like cell line increased histone acetylation.
source: This result was unlikely to be an indirect result of cardiac dysfunction in EedCKO hearts, because a similar effect was observed after acute, siRNA-mediated Eed knockdown in the HL-1 CM-like cell line (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data from HL-1 cells.

claim: Eed inactivation led to acquisition of 8161 new H3K27ac sites.
source: Genome-wide H3K27ac occupancy analysis by ChIP-seq in 2-month-old WT or EedCKO purified CMs showed that Eed inactivation led to acquisition of 8161 new H3K27ac sites and loss of 5950 sites, with 20799 sites in common (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq peak analysis.

claim: Eed inactivation led to loss of 5950 H3K27ac sites.
source: Genome-wide H3K27ac occupancy analysis by ChIP-seq in 2-month-old WT or EedCKO purified CMs showed that Eed inactivation led to acquisition of 8161 new H3K27ac sites and loss of 5950 sites, with 20799 sites in common (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq peak analysis.

claim: 20799 H3K27ac sites were in common between WT and EedCKO.
source: Genome-wide H3K27ac occupancy analysis by ChIP-seq in 2-month-old WT or EedCKO purified CMs showed that Eed inactivation led to acquisition of 8161 new H3K27ac sites and loss of 5950 sites, with 20799 sites in common (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq peak analysis.

claim: Eed inactivation caused a broad, genome-wide increase of H3K27ac signal strength.
source: These peak changes were accompanied by a broad, genome-wide increase of H3K27ac signal strength (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal distribution analysis.

claim: The aggregate H3K27ac signal at the promoters of the 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO increased.
source: Indeed, the aggregate H3K27ac signal at the promoters of the 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO increased, whereas it was either unchanged or reduced for the genes that were unchanged or downregulated, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by aggregate plot analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-seq data.

claim: Increased H3K27ac signal was observed at enhancer regions associated with upregulated genes in EedCKO.
source: Increased H3K27ac signal was also observed at enhancer regions (H3K27ac peaks region in either WT or EedCKO) associated with these upregulated genes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by aggregate plot analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-seq data at enhancers.

claim: All 863 derepressed genes markedly gained H3K27ac levels.
source: Heatmap analysis of all three clusters and quantitative analysis in box plots for each cluster confirmed that all 863 derepressed genes markedly gained H3K27ac levels (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by heatmap and box plot analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-seq data.

claim: EED is required to suppress H3K27ac.
source: Together these data suggest that EED is required to suppress H3K27ac, and that loss of this function leads to abnormal H3K27ac accumulation, global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation, and aberrant gene upregulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased H3K27ac upon EED loss.

claim: Loss of EED function leads to abnormal H3K27ac accumulation.
source: Together these data suggest that EED is required to suppress H3K27ac, and that loss of this function leads to abnormal H3K27ac accumulation, global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation, and aberrant gene upregulation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and immunoblotting data showing increased H3K27ac in EedCKO.

claim: Loss of EED function leads to global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation.
source: Together these data suggest that EED is required to suppress H3K27ac, and that loss of this function leads to abnormal H3K27ac accumulation, global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation, and aberrant gene upregulation.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Loss of EED function leads to aberrant gene upregulation.
source: Together these data suggest that EED is required to suppress H3K27ac, and that loss of this function leads to abnormal H3K27ac accumulation, global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation, and aberrant gene upregulation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing gene upregulation in EedCKO.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression at P14 or P25 rescued cardiac systolic function of EedCKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, delayed EED re-expression was still able to rescue cardiac systolic function and cardiac hypertrophy, normalize expression of myofiber and heart failure genes, and ameliorate cardiomegaly of EedCKO mutants (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression at P14 or P25 rescued cardiac hypertrophy of EedCKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, delayed EED re-expression was still able to rescue cardiac systolic function and cardiac hypertrophy, normalize expression of myofiber and heart failure genes, and ameliorate cardiomegaly of EedCKO mutants (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by heart weight and histological data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression at P14 or P25 normalized expression of myofiber and heart failure genes in EedCKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, delayed EED re-expression was still able to rescue cardiac systolic function and cardiac hypertrophy, normalize expression of myofiber and heart failure genes, and ameliorate cardiomegaly of EedCKO mutants (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression at P14 or P25 ameliorated cardiomegaly of EedCKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, delayed EED re-expression was still able to rescue cardiac systolic function and cardiac hypertrophy, normalize expression of myofiber and heart failure genes, and ameliorate cardiomegaly of EedCKO mutants (Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by gross morphology and heart weight data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression corrected the abnormally high global H3K27ac levels observed in EedCKO.
source: Delayed EED re-expression corrected the abnormally high global H3K27ac levels observed in EedCKO (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Delayed EED re-expression did not correct the low H3K27me3 levels seen in EedCKO.
source: However, delayed EED re-expression did not correct the low H3K27me3 levels seen in EedCKO (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: EED re-expression at P14 and P25 both conferred phenotypic rescue and normalized the genome-wide distribution of H3K27ac signal.
source: Whereas EED re-expression at P14 and P25 both conferred phenotypic rescue and normalized the genome-wide distribution of H3K27ac signal, P14 and P25 EED re-expression did not normalize H3K27me3 distribution (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: P14 and P25 EED re-expression did not normalize H3K27me3 distribution.
source: Whereas EED re-expression at P14 and P25 both conferred phenotypic rescue and normalized the genome-wide distribution of H3K27ac signal, P14 and P25 EED re-expression did not normalize H3K27me3 distribution (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Out of 863 genes that were upregulated in EedCKO, 256 were significantly downregulated by AAV-EED rescue.
source: Out of 863 genes that were upregulated in EedCKO, 256 (66, 87, and 103 in Cluster 1, 2, and 3, respectively) were significantly downregulated (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: Normalization of gene expression by AAV-EED was associated with reduction of H3K27ac, but not H3K27me3, near the TSS.
source: This normalization of gene expression was associated with reduction of H3K27ac, but not H3K27me3, near the TSS (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from AAV-EED rescue experiments.

claim: At the upregulated slow twitch skeletal muscle genes, delayed EED re-expression corrected abnormal deposition of H3K27ac but did not significantly affect H3K27me3.
source: Inspection of the Acta1 and Myl7 loci reinforced the finding that, at the upregulated slow twitch skeletal muscle genes, delayed EED re-expression corrected abnormal deposition of H3K27ac but did not significantly affect H3K27me3 (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by genome browser view of ChIP-seq data at specific loci.

claim: Phenotypic rescue and gene expression correction by AAV-EED were not associated with normalization of H3K27me3.
source: Regardless of the precise mechanism, our data show that phenotypic rescue and gene expression correction by AAV-EED were not associated with normalization of H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive analysis of rescue experiments showing functional correction without H3K27me3 restoration.

claim: Correction by AAV-EED aligned with normalization of H3K27ac epigenetic marks.
source: Rather, correction aligned with normalization of H3K27ac epigenetic marks.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing H3K27ac normalization in rescue experiments.

claim: EedCKO hearts had elevated global histone H3 and H4 acetylation but total HDAC levels were not changed.
source: Although EedCKO hearts had elevated global histone H3 and H4 acetylation, most strikingly inducing H3K27ac, total HDAC levels were not changed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunoblotting data.

claim: HDAC2 interacts with EED.
source: Otte and colleagues showed that HDAC2 interacts with EED and that EED co-immunoprecipitated protein complexes containing HDAC activity (van der Vlag and Otte, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: EED co-immunoprecipitated protein complexes containing HDAC activity.
source: Otte and colleagues showed that HDAC2 interacts with EED and that EED co-immunoprecipitated protein complexes containing HDAC activity (van der Vlag and Otte, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of FLAG-tagged HDAC1-HDAC9 co-precipitated HA-tagged EED, with the exception of HDAC8.
source: Immunoprecipitation of FLAG-tagged HDAC1-HDAC9 co-precipitated HA-tagged EED, with the exception of HDAC8 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: HA-EED co-precipitated HDAC1-HDAC9 except HDAC8 in reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: This was confirmed by reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments, in which HA-EED co-precipitated HDAC1-HDAC9 except HDAC8 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Endogenous EED and HDAC2 interact in HL-1 CM-like cells.
source: We further confirmed the interaction of endogenous EED and HDAC2 in HL-1 CM-like cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous proteins.

claim: Nearly half of HDAC2 peaks (4042 out of 9869, 41%) overlapped with EED peaks in WT.
source: Nearly half of HDAC2 peaks (4042 out of 9869, 41%) overlapped with EED peaks in WT, in line with their biochemical interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq peak overlap analysis.

claim: Overall, HDAC2 signals did not change in EED deficient CMs.
source: Overall, HDAC2 signals did not change in EED deficient CMs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by aggregate plot analysis of HDAC2 ChIP-seq data.

claim: HDAC2 or HDAC5 occupancy at promoters of genes upregulated in EedCKO did not differ significantly from control.
source: This finding was also confirmed by ChIP-qPCR measurement of HDAC2 or HDAC5 enrichment at promoters of genes upregulated in EedCKO compared to control, revealing no significant difference between HDAC2 or HDAC5 occupancy (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: Eed inactivation did not change HDAC2 occupancy.
source: This analysis reinforced that Eed inactivation did not change HDAC2 occupancy, indicating that HDAC2 accumulation on genomic domains is independent of EED (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis of HDAC2 occupancy at different gene classes.

claim: HDAC2 accumulation on genomic domains is independent of EED.
source: This analysis reinforced that Eed inactivation did not change HDAC2 occupancy, indicating that HDAC2 accumulation on genomic domains is independent of EED (Figure 4G).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of change in HDAC2 occupancy upon EED loss.

claim: Elevated acetylation on H3K27ac in EedCKO was unlikely due to decreased HDAC binding.
source: Thus, elevated acetylation on H3K27ac in EedCKO was unlikely due to decreased HDAC binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HDAC occupancy did not change in EedCKO.

claim: EED augmented HDAC2's deacetylase activity by up to threefold in vitro.
source: EED alone had no detectable deacetylase activity, but when added to HDAC2 it augmented HDAC2's deacetylase activity by up to threefold (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro deacetylase activity assay.

claim: EED alone had no detectable deacetylase activity.
source: EED alone had no detectable deacetylase activity, but when added to HDAC2 it augmented HDAC2's deacetylase activity by up to threefold (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in vitro deacetylase activity assay.

claim: EED represses a subset of its target genes by stimulating HDAC.
source: Together, the aforementioned data all support a model in which EED represses a subset of its target genes by stimulating HDAC.
evidence: Inferred from the biochemical interaction, co-occupancy, and activity enhancement data.

claim: EED drives transcriptional repression at least partially by modulating the activity of HDACs.
source: These results also raise the possibility that EED drives transcriptional repression at least partially by modulating the activity of another class of epigenetic repressors, HDACs.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing EED-HDAC interaction and activity enhancement.

claim: Cardiac-restricted deletion of both HDAC1 and HDAC2 caused dilated cardiomyopathy accompanied by upregulation of genes encoding skeletal muscle-specific contractile proteins.
source: Notably, cardiac-restricted deletion of both HDAC1 and HDAC2 caused dilated cardiomyopathy accompanied by upregulation of genes encoding skeletal muscle-specific contractile proteins (Montgomery et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: AAV-HDAC1/2 delivery to P3 EedCKO mice normalized systolic dysfunction.
source: Remarkably, AAV-HDAC1/2 delivery to P3 EedCKO mice (CKO-HDAC1/2) normalized systolic dysfunction and cardiomegaly, compared to control treatment with luciferase (CKO-luc; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: AAV-HDAC1/2 delivery to P3 EedCKO mice normalized cardiomegaly.
source: Remarkably, AAV-HDAC1/2 delivery to P3 EedCKO mice (CKO-HDAC1/2) normalized systolic dysfunction and cardiomegaly, compared to control treatment with luciferase (CKO-luc; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by heart weight and gross morphology data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: AAV-HDAC1/2 restored repression of slow twitch sarcomere genes Acta1 and Myh7.
source: AAV-HDAC1/2 also restored repression of slow twitch sarcomere genes Acta1 and Myh7, and reduced expression of the heart failure marker Nppa (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: AAV-HDAC1/2 reduced expression of the heart failure marker Nppa.
source: AAV-HDAC1/2 also restored repression of slow twitch sarcomere genes Acta1 and Myh7, and reduced expression of the heart failure marker Nppa (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: Out of 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO, 104 were downregulated by AAV-HDAC1/2.
source: RNA-seq gene expression measurements showed that out of 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO, 104 were downregulated in the rescue group (adjusted p-value<0.05 and fold change (CKO-luc/CKO-HDAC1/2) >1.5; Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: The greater H3K27ac signal observed at the TSS of most of the 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO was normalized by AAV-HDAC1/2.
source: This revealed that the greater H3K27ac signal observed at the TSS of most of the 863 genes upregulated in EedCKO was normalized by AAV-HDAC1/2: the ratio of H3K27ac signal in CKO-luc to CKO-HDAC1/2 was ≥1.5 for 460 genes and 1–1.5 for 293 genes, while only 110 were not changed (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: Within each of the three classes of regions (C1, C2, C3), AAV-HDAC1/2 significantly reduced H3K27ac signal.
source: Within each of the three classes of regions (C1, C2, C3) defined previously based on H3K27ac occupancy and change with Eed inactivation (Figure 1J), AAV-HDAC1/2 significantly reduced H3K27ac signal.
evidence: Supported by box plot analysis of H3K27ac ChIP-seq data.

claim: H3K27me3 was not strongly affected by AAV-HDAC1/2.
source: On the other hand, H3K27me3 was not strongly affected by AAV-HDAC1/2 (Figure 5E–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and immunoblotting data from AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue experiments.

claim: Heart function normalization by AAV-HDAC1/2 was not dependent upon broad normalization of H3K27ac but rather on targeted HDAC1/2 activity at specific loci.
source: Thus, heart function normalization was not dependent upon broad normalization of H3K27ac but rather on targeted HDAC1/2 activity at specific loci.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that global H3K27ac levels did not change but specific loci were normalized.

claim: Correction of gene expression and heart function by AAV-HDAC1/2 was independent of H3K27me3.
source: On the other hand, H3K27me3 was not strongly affected by AAV-HDAC1/2 (Figure 5E–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G), consistent with the findings in EED rescue experiments that correction of gene expression and heart function was independent of H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing no change in H3K27me3 with AAV-HDAC1/2 rescue.

claim: SAHA treatment for 2 months did not adversely affect heart function in Het controls.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Xie et al., 2014b), SAHA treatment for 2 months did not adversely effect heart function in the Het controls, nor did it perturb expression of 5 genes (Acta1, Myl9, Tnni1, Tbx15 and Mybpc2) that were aberrantly upregulated in EedCKO.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography and gene expression data from SAHA treatment experiments.

claim: SAHA treatment did not perturb expression of 5 genes (Acta1, Myl9, Tnni1, Tbx15 and Mybpc2) that were aberrantly upregulated in EedCKO in Het controls.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Xie et al., 2014b), SAHA treatment for 2 months did not adversely effect heart function in the Het controls, nor did it perturb expression of 5 genes (Acta1, Myl9, Tnni1, Tbx15 and Mybpc2) that were aberrantly upregulated in EedCKO.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from SAHA treatment experiments.

claim: SAHA treatment appeared to block heart function rescue by AAV9-EED re-expression.
source: Interestingly, SAHA treatment appeared to block heart function rescue by AAV9-EED re-expression.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data showing reduced rescue effect with SAHA treatment.

claim: Normalized transcription of four out of five genes by EED re-expression in EedCKO was blocked by SAHA treatment.
source: In line with this, normalized transcription of four out of five genes by EED re-expression in EedCKO was blocked by SAHA treatment (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from SAHA treatment experiments.

claim: HDAC activity is essential to suppress aberrant gene expression in EedCKO.
source: These data suggest that HDAC activity is essential to suppress aberrant gene expression in EedCKO.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HDAC inhibition blocked rescue by EED re-expression.

claim: Normalization of HDAC activity by EED re-expression was essential for rescue of heart failure in EedCKO.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that normalization of HDAC activity by EED re-expression was essential for rescue of heart failure in EedCKO.
evidence: Inferred from the SAHA inhibition experiments showing requirement of HDAC activity for rescue.

claim: HDACs collaborate with EED to mediate postnatal cardiac gene repression required for normal heart development and function.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that HDACs collaborate with EED to mediate postnatal cardiac gene repression required for normal heart development and function.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive set of experiments showing EED-HDAC interaction, activity enhancement, and rescue effects.

claim: EED functions genetically upstream of HDACs.
source: Furthermore, our data indicate that EED functions genetically upstream of HDACs and support a model in which EED maintains transcriptional repression of target genes in post-mitotic cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HDAC overexpression can rescue EED deficiency.

claim: EED maintains transcriptional repression of target genes in post-mitotic cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, our data indicate that EED functions genetically upstream of HDACs and support a model in which EED maintains transcriptional repression of target genes in post-mitotic cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive data showing EED's role in gene repression in postnatal cardiomyocytes.

claim: An essential mechanism of EED repression is independent of its requirement for PRC2 deposition of H3K27me3.
source: Our results demonstrate an essential mechanism of EED repression that is independent of its requirement for PRC2 deposition of H3K27me3 (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive data showing gene repression and rescue without H3K27me3 changes.

claim: Postnatal loss of EED caused lethal dilated cardiomyopathy associated with ectopic expression of a slow skeletal muscle gene program.
source: We found that postnatal loss of EED caused lethal dilated cardiomyopathy associated with ecoptic expression of a slow skeletal muscle gene program.
evidence: Supported by survival, echocardiography, and RNA-seq data.

claim: De-repression of the slow skeletal muscle gene program was not associated with loss of H3K27me3 at these genes.
source: Surprisingly, de-repression of this program was not associated with loss of H3K27me3 at these genes, but rather marked gain of H3K27ac.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing unchanged H3K27me3 but increased H3K27ac at upregulated genes.

claim: De-repression of the slow skeletal muscle gene program was associated with marked gain of H3K27ac.
source: Surprisingly, de-repression of this program was not associated with loss of H3K27me3 at these genes, but rather marked gain of H3K27ac.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing increased H3K27ac at upregulated genes.

claim: EED depletion caused global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation.
source: Moreover, EED depletion caused global increase in histone H3 and H4 acetylation.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Phenotypic reversal was associated with normalization of H3K27ac but not H3K27me3.
source: Our rescue experiments further demonstrated that phenotypic reversal was associated with normalization of H3K27ac but not H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and immunoblotting data from rescue experiments.

claim: There is a physical and genetic interaction between EED and HDACs.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate a physical and genetic interaction between EED and HDACs that mechanistically accounts, at least in part, for the link between EED loss of function and aberrant H3K27ac accumulation.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation, activity assays, and rescue experiments.

claim: The physical and genetic interaction between EED and HDACs mechanistically accounts, at least in part, for the link between EED loss of function and aberrant H3K27ac accumulation.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate a physical and genetic interaction between EED and HDACs that mechanistically accounts, at least in part, for the link between EED loss of function and aberrant H3K27ac accumulation.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data showing EED-HDAC interaction and its effects on H3K27ac.

claim: Disease caused by aberrant epigenetic regulation can be reversed through epigenetic rewiring.
source: Together these experiments highlight an H3K27me3-independent repressive activity of EED, and demonstrate that disease caused by aberrant epigenetic regulation can be reversed through epigenetic rewiring.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing functional correction without restoring the original epigenetic landscape.

claim: Most studies of PRC2 function have been performed in actively cycling cells.
source: Furthermore, most studies of PRC2 function have been performed in actively cycling cells, whereas the majority of cells in adult mammals cycle slowly, and some cells, such as adult cardiomyocytes (CMs), are largely post-mitotic.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about PRC2 studies and cardiomyocyte biology.

claim: The majority of cells in adult mammals cycle slowly.
source: Furthermore, most studies of PRC2 function have been performed in actively cycling cells, whereas the majority of cells in adult mammals cycle slowly, and some cells, such as adult cardiomyocytes (CMs), are largely post-mitotic.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about cell biology in adult mammals.

claim: Adult cardiomyocytes are largely post-mitotic.
source: Furthermore, most studies of PRC2 function have been performed in actively cycling cells, whereas the majority of cells in adult mammals cycle slowly, and some cells, such as adult cardiomyocytes (CMs), are largely post-mitotic.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about cardiomyocyte biology.

claim: Cell cycle activity mandates re-deposition of histone marks.
source: Since cell cycle activity mandates re-deposition of histone marks (Margueron et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2008), in mitotic cells writing activity of epigenetic complexes may overshadow other functions that are important in non-proliferating cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mitotic cells writing activity of epigenetic complexes may overshadow other functions that are important in non-proliferating cells.
source: Since cell cycle activity mandates re-deposition of histone marks (Margueron et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2008), in mitotic cells writing activity of epigenetic complexes may overshadow other functions that are important in non-proliferating cells.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for histone mark re-deposition in cycling cells.

claim: Postnatal CMs have largely exited the cell cycle.
source: Postnatal CMs have largely exited the cell cycle (Bergmann et al., 2009, Bergmann et al., 2015; Senyo et al., 2013; Ali et al., 2014; Alkass et al., 2015; Soonpaa et al., 2015; Hirai et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Postnatal CMs express little EZH2 protein.
source: Postnatal CMs have largely exited the cell cycle (Bergmann et al., 2009, Bergmann et al., 2015; Senyo et al., 2013; Ali et al., 2014; Alkass et al., 2015; Soonpaa et al., 2015; Hirai et al., 2016) and express little EZH2 protein (He et al., 2012a)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Postnatal CMs contain abundant H3K27me3.
source: Postnatal CMs have largely exited the cell cycle (Bergmann et al., 2009, Bergmann et al., 2015; Senyo et al., 2013; Ali et al., 2014; Alkass et al., 2015; Soonpaa et al., 2015; Hirai et al., 2016) and express little EZH2 protein (He et al., 2012a), but nonetheless contain abundant H3K27me3.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and ChIP-seq data in the study.

claim: EED silences the slow-twitch myofiber gene program to orchestrate heart maturation by complexing with and stimulating HDAC deacetylase activity.
source: We found that EED silences the slow-twitch myofiber gene program to orchestrate heart maturation by complexing with and stimulating HDAC deacetylase activity.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive data showing EED-HDAC interaction, activity enhancement, and effects on gene expression.

claim: De-repression of the majority of genes in EED-deficient cardiomyocytes occurred without loss of H3K27me3.
source: Surprising, de-repression of the majority of genes in EED-deficient cardiomyocytes occurred without loss of H3K27me3, pointing to important EED repressive activity that is independent of its role in PRC2-mediated H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing unchanged H3K27me3 at most upregulated genes.

claim: EED has important repressive activity that is independent of its role in PRC2-mediated H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Surprising, de-repression of the majority of genes in EED-deficient cardiomyocytes occurred without loss of H3K27me3, pointing to important EED repressive activity that is independent of its role in PRC2-mediated H3K27 trimethylation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that gene derepression occurred without H3K27me3 loss.
